slides.heading: Sorted Squared Array
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Easy · Arrays
slides.narration: Let's solve Sorted Squared Array, an easy arrays problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Given a sorted array (may contain negatives) return the squares in sorted order.
Two pointers from both ends fill the result from the back.
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Given a sorted array (may contain negatives) return the squares in sorted order. Two pointers from both ends fill the result from the back.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: The largest squares sit at the two ends of a sorted array, because big negatives square to big positives.
slides.narration: The largest squares sit at the two ends of a sorted array, because big negatives square to big positives.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Brute force: square everything, then sort → O(n log n)
Optimal: largest squares are at the ends → two pointers, O(n)
slides.narration: The brute-force approach squares every value and sorts the result, which is n log n. But since the input is sorted, the largest square must come from one of the two ends, so two pointers fill the output from the back in linear time.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. Put pointers at both ends
2. Compare absolute values
3. Write the larger square into the result from the back
4. Move that pointer inward
slides.narration: Step by step. First, put pointers at both ends. Second, compare absolute values. Third, write the larger square into the result from the back. Fourth, move that pointer inward.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: |8| is larger → write 64 at index 4
slides.narration: Compare the absolute values at the two ends. The right one, 8, is larger, so its square, 64, goes into position 4, and we move that pointer inward.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: |-7| is larger → write 49 at index 3
slides.narration: Compare the absolute values at the two ends. The left one, -7, is larger, so its square, 49, goes into position 3, and we move that pointer inward.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: |4| is larger → write 16 at index 2
slides.narration: Compare the absolute values at the two ends. The right one, 4, is larger, so its square, 16, goes into position 2, and we move that pointer inward.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: |-3| is larger → write 9 at index 1
slides.narration: Compare the absolute values at the two ends. The left one, -3, is larger, so its square, 9, goes into position 1, and we move that pointer inward.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: |1| is larger → write 1 at index 0
slides.narration: Compare the absolute values at the two ends. The right one, 1, is larger, so its square, 1, goes into position 0, and we move that pointer inward.

slides.heading: Java solution
slides.narration: We keep left and right pointers and an output array. Walking k from the last index down, we compare absolute values at both ends, write the larger square at k, and move that pointer inward.

slides.heading: Complexity
bullets: Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
slides.narration: Time is O of n. Space is O of n.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: All negatives: squares come out reversed
Zeros and duplicates are fine
Fill the output from the back, not the front
Don't modify the input in place
slides.narration: Watch out for an all-negative input, where the order fully reverses, and remember that the output must be filled from the back, because we always find the largest remaining square.

slides.heading: Interview tips & follow-ups
bullets: State the brute force first, then improve
Follow-up: do it in place? (not easily — need extra array)
Generalise: merge of two sorted sequences
slides.narration: Mention the sort-based solution first, then improve it. This is really a merge of two sorted sequences, the negatives reversed and the non-negatives, which is a nice way to explain it.

slides.heading: Recap
bullets: The largest squares sit at the two ends of a sorted array, because big negatives square to big positives.
Complexity: O(n)
slides.narration: To recap Sorted Squared Array: The largest squares sit at the two ends of a sorted array, because big negatives square to big positives. Try re-implementing it from scratch without looking.
